core: Kinematics: position, displacement, velocity, acceleration as vectors
Distance versus displacement; speed versus velocity
Constant-acceleration equations and the constant-acceleration assumption
Newton's first law and its role in defining an inertial reference frame
Newton's second law: sum of external forces equals mass times acceleration for constant mass; the momentum form as the general statement
Newton's third law and the fact that the paired forces act on different bodies
Mass versus weight; the newton; g treated as an acceleration; the defined standard acceleration of gravity
Common force types: gravitational, normal, tension, friction (static and kinetic), applied
Net force and equilibrium as the special case of zero net force
The Aristotelian misconception that sustained motion requires a sustained force
Idealizations: point mass, rigid body, massless rope, frictionless pulley, constant g, constant mass — and where each fails
supporting: SI base and coherent derived units relevant to mechanics
Pound-force and kilogram-force conversions to the newton
Significant figures in a multi-step mechanics calculation
The empirical, approximate character of the friction coefficient model
outOfScope: Rigid-body equilibrium, moments, trusses and supports — owned by the statics topic
Kinetics of systems, projectile and circular motion problem sets — owned by the dynamics topic
Work, kinetic and potential energy, power — owned by the work-and-energy topic
Impulse, conservation of momentum, collisions — owned by the momentum topic
Relativistic and quantum corrections to Newtonian mechanics
Specific engineering design values, allowable stresses, or factors of safety

claims.claim: Displacement is the vector change in position and its magnitude can be smaller than the distance travelled, which is the length of the path actually followed; a closed loop gives zero displacement and non-zero distance.

Instantaneous speed is the magnitude of instantaneous velocity, and average speed (total distance over elapsed time) is not in general equal to the magnitude of average velocity (total displacement over elapsed time).

The standard kinematic relations v = v0 + a t, x = x0 + v0 t + a t^2 / 2, v^2 = v0^2 + 2 a (x - x0), and x = x0 + v-bar t with v-bar = (v0 + v)/2 are derived on the explicit assumption that acceleration is constant, and are not valid where the acceleration varies.

Newton's first law states that a body at rest stays at rest and a body in motion continues at constant velocity unless acted on by a net external force, and an inertial reference frame is one in which that law holds; frames moving at constant velocity relative to an inertial frame are also inertial while accelerating frames are not.

Newton's second law relates acceleration to the net EXTERNAL force divided by mass; internal forces cancel and do not affect the motion of the system. The familiar F_net = m a is the constant-mass case of Newton's general statement F_net = dp/dt.
Newton's third law pairs consist of forces of equal magnitude and opposite direction that act on two different bodies, and for that reason they are distinct forces that do not cancel each other.

Mass does not vary with location while weight does; weight is the force w = m g, and on the Moon, where g is about 1.62 m/s^2, a 1.0 kg mass weighs about 1.6 N against about 9.8 N on Earth. Local g varies slightly over Earth's surface.

In science and technology the weight of a body is the force that gives it an acceleration equal to the local acceleration of free fall, with the newton as its unit, whereas in everyday and commercial usage 'weight' means mass and is expressed in kilograms; NIST directs technical writers to use 'mass' when mass is meant and to make the sense explicit whenever 'weight' is used.
The newton is the SI coherent derived unit of force, with the expression m . kg . s^-2 in SI base units.
One pound-force equals 4.448 222 newtons and one kilogram-force equals 9.806 65 newtons, per the NIST conversion tables.

The standard acceleration of gravity g_n is 9.806 65 m/s^2 and is an exact, defined conventional value — adopted as 980.665 cm/s^2 by the 3rd CGPM in 1901 — rather than a measurement of the local gravitational field.

The friction coefficient model — static friction bounded by f_s <= mu_s N and kinetic friction modelled as f_k = mu_k N — is an approximate empirical model that treats friction as independent of contact area, and kinetic coefficients are generally smaller than their static counterparts.

Equilibrium in engineering usage means zero acceleration, expressed as the vector sum of forces equal to zero, and it covers a body moving at constant velocity as well as one at rest; the condition follows directly from Newton's second law.

Worked example arithmetic: for m = 24.0 kg and g = 9.81 m/s^2, w = 235.44 N; with an assumed mu_s = 0.45 the maximum static friction is 105.948 N, so a 96.0 N push does not move the crate; with an assumed mu_k = 0.35 the kinetic friction is 82.404 N, a 118 N push gives a net 35.596 N and a = 1.48317 m/s^2, reported to two significant figures as 1.5 m/s^2; from rest after 1.50 s, v = 2.22475 m/s (2.2 m/s) and displacement = 1.66856 m (1.7 m).

Question-bank arithmetic: 400 m / 80.0 s = 5.00 m/s; 12 kg x 9.81 m/s^2 = 117.72 N (about 118 N) and 12 kg x 1.62 m/s^2 = 19.44 N (about 19 N); (22 N - 9.0 N) / 5.0 kg = 2.6 m/s^2, while the distractors 6.2 m/s^2 and 1.8 m/s^2 come from 31 N / 5.0 kg and 9.0 N / 5.0 kg respectively.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What value of g to use in worked calculations.
positions: OpenStax University Physics uses g = 9.80 m/s^2 as a working value near Earth's surface and notes that local g varies.
NIST and the 3rd CGPM (1901) give the standard acceleration of gravity as exactly 9.806 65 m/s^2, a defined conventional value.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson separates the two ideas explicitly: it uses g = 9.81 m/s^2 as a rounded local working value in the worked example, and states that g_n = 9.806 65 m/s^2 is a defined constant used for conversions, not a measurement of any particular location's field. Both figures are attributed to the right source.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether Newton's first law is redundant given the second law.
positions: Read purely as a statement about bodies, the first law is the second law with zero net force.
Read as a statement about frames of reference, the first law identifies which frames the second law is valid in.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson gives both readings and says plainly that the frame-defining reading is the one that earns the first law its separate status, consistent with the OpenStax treatment of inertial reference frames.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether friction coefficients can be quoted as reliable values.
positions: Textbook tables list representative coefficients for material pairs.
The coefficient model is explicitly described by its own sources as an approximate empirical model, and real values depend on finish, contamination, wear, speed, and pressure.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The worked example labels its coefficients as assumed problem data and does not attribute them to any source or standard, and the lesson states the model's limits directly.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's framing of 'Force And Motion' as an abstract organising concept, with no physics content at all: no kinematic quantities, no laws, no units, no forces.
The draft's vocabulary entries ('context', 'evidence', 'application') and its self-referential definition of the topic term, none of which describe anything in mechanics.
The draft's toolbox-drawer analogy and map-legend analogy, neither of which teaches anything about force or motion.
The draft's worked example, which contained no worked quantity and no calculation.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generated draft with subject-specific content; nothing from the draft's wording survives.
Stated Newton's second law as a sum over EXTERNAL forces and flagged F = ma as the constant-mass case of F = dp/dt, which most introductory treatments elide.
Put the different-bodies point of the third law in Common Mistakes, as the assignment requires, rather than leaving it as a passing remark.
Named the Aristotelian intuition explicitly as the misconception Newton's first law replaces.
Separated the working value g = 9.81 m/s^2 from the defined standard value g_n = 9.806 65 m/s^2 and stated that g is an acceleration, not a force.
Wrote static friction as an inequality throughout and labelled the coefficient model as approximate and empirical, per its own source.
Handed off free-body diagram construction, statics, dynamics, work and energy, and momentum to their own topics rather than teaching them here.
Carried units through every step of the worked example and rounded the reported answers to the two significant figures the assumed coefficients justify.
Added the subject's required educational-material and not-engineering-design-guidance statement.
rightsIssues: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1 per-book reuse terms were not verified for this project, so all six OpenStax pages are held at REFERENCE_ONLY and no wording from them is reproduced.
The Engineering Statics (Baker and Haynes) LibreTexts page carries CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, a non-commercial licence, so it is used as a factual reference only and no text is adapted.

The BIPM SI Brochure landing page states a CC BY 4.0 licence, but the brochure PDF could not be parsed by the fetcher; the record is held at REFERENCE_ONLY and the newton's base-unit expression is instead cited to NIST SP 811 Chapter 4, which was read directly.
NIST SP 811 pages are U.S. Government works, but no per-page reuse statement was located, so they are held at REFERENCE_ONLY and the lesson states the facts in its own words.
No engineering standard (ASME, ASTM, ISO, AISC, ACI, IEEE) text, table, or design value is reproduced or relied on anywhere in this lesson.

sourceRecords.title: University Physics Volume 1, 3.1 Position, Displacement, and Average Velocity
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live page. Supports the definitions of position, displacement as the vector change in position, total displacement as the sum of individual displacements, distance travelled as the length of the path actually followed, and average velocity as total displacement over elapsed time. Per-book reuse terms were not verified for this subject, so the record is held at REFERENCE_ONLY and no wording from the page is reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: University Physics Volume 1, 3.2 Instantaneous Velocity and Speed
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live page. Supports the statement that instantaneous speed is the magnitude of instantaneous velocity, and that average speed (total distance over elapsed time) is not in general the magnitude of average velocity — the page uses a round trip, where average velocity is zero and average speed is not, to make the point. REFERENCE_ONLY; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: University Physics Volume 1, 3.4 Motion with Constant Acceleration
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live page. Supports the set of constant-acceleration equations quoted in the lesson (v = v0 + at; x = x0 + v0 t + at^2/2; v^2 = v0^2 + 2a(x - x0); x = x0 + v-bar t with v-bar = (v0 + v)/2) and the page's explicit statement that the derivation rests on assuming acceleration is constant. REFERENCE_ONLY; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: University Physics Volume 1, 5.2 Newton's First Law
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live page. Supports the statement of the first law, inertia as resistance to acceleration measured by mass, and the definition of an inertial reference frame as one in which the first law holds, with frames moving at constant velocity relative to an inertial frame also inertial and accelerating frames not. REFERENCE_ONLY; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: University Physics Volume 1, 5.3 Newton's Second Law
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live page. Supports the vector form a = F_net/m and its rearrangement F_net = m a, the restriction of the sum to external forces, and the page's own statement that Newton stated the second law in terms of momentum, F_net = dp/dt, which reduces to F_net = m a when mass is constant. REFERENCE_ONLY; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: University Physics Volume 1, 5.4 Mass and Weight
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live page. Supports w = m g, the statement that mass does not vary with location while weight does, the approximate value g = 9.80 m/s^2 near Earth's surface, the caution that g varies slightly over Earth's surface, and the Moon comparison (g about 1.62 m/s^2, so a 1.0 kg mass weighs about 1.6 N there against about 9.8 N on Earth). REFERENCE_ONLY; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: University Physics Volume 1, 5.5 Newton's Third Law
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live page. Supports the statement of the third law and, critically for this lesson's Common Mistakes section, the page's explicit insistence that the two forces act on different bodies, are therefore distinct forces, and do not cancel each other; the swimmer-and-pool-wall example is the page's own illustration of the point. REFERENCE_ONLY; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: University Physics Volume 1, 6.2 Friction
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live page. Supports the coefficient model, static friction as the inequality f_s <= mu_s N and kinetic friction as f_k = mu_k N, the page's explicit characterisation of these relations as an approximate empirical model only, the modelled independence from contact area, and the general result that kinetic coefficients are smaller than their static counterparts. REFERENCE_ONLY; no wording reproduced. No coefficient value in the lesson is taken from this page — the worked example's coefficients are stated as assumed problem data.

sourceRecords.title: Engineering Statics: Open and Interactive, 3.1 Equilibrium
sourceRecords.provider: Daniel W. Baker and William Haynes, Colorado State University, hosted on Engineering LibreTexts
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live page. Supports the engineering framing of equilibrium as zero acceleration (body stationary or moving at constant velocity), the equilibrium condition written as the vector sum of forces equal to zero, its derivation from Newton's second law, and the point that choosing which body to isolate is an engineering decision. The page carries CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, which is non-commercial and therefore not relied on for reuse here; held at REFERENCE_ONLY and no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: NIST Guide to the SI, Chapter 4: The Two Classes of SI Units and the SI Prefixes

sourceRecords.notes: Read the live page. REFERENCE_ONLY; the lesson states the fact and does not reproduce the table.

sourceRecords.title: NIST Guide to the SI, Chapter 8: Comments on Some Quantities and Their Units
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST Special Publication 811, 2008 edition)
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live page. Section 8.3 supports the lesson's mass-versus-weight treatment: in science and technology the weight of a body is the force that gives it an acceleration equal to the local acceleration of free fall, with the newton as its unit, while in everyday and commercial usage 'weight' means mass and is quoted in kilograms; the guide instructs writers to say mass when they mean mass and to make the intended sense explicit whenever they use 'weight'. REFERENCE_ONLY; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: NIST Guide to the SI, Appendix B.9: Conversion Factors Listed by Kind of Quantity
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST Special Publication 811, 2008 edition)
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live page. Under FORCE the guide lists pound-force (lbf) to newton as 4.448 222 E+00 and kilogram-force (kgf) to newton as 9.806 65 E+00; these are the conversion factors quoted in the lesson. REFERENCE_ONLY.

sourceRecords.title: Standard acceleration of gravity (g_n) — CODATA value page
sourceRecords.provider: NIST Physical Measurement Laboratory, Fundamental Physical Constants
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live page. Gives the standard acceleration of gravity as 9.806 65 m s^-2 and marks the value exact (no uncertainty), which is the basis for the lesson's statement that g_n is a defined conventional value rather than a measurement of any particular location's field.

sourceRecords.title: Resolution 2 of the 3rd CGPM (1901): Declaration on the unit of mass and on the definition of weight; conventional value of g_n
sourceRecords.provider: Bureau International des Poids et Mesures (BIPM), Conference generale des poids et mesures
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live page. The 1901 resolution adopts 980.665 cm/s^2 (that is, 9.806 65 m/s^2) as the value of the standard acceleration due to gravity for the International Service of Weights and Measures. Used for the lesson's claim that g_n is a conventional value fixed by the 3rd CGPM in 1901, not a measured local field.
